title: WHAT IF THE PERSON WHO PROMISED TO LOVE YOU FOREVER LOOKS YOU IN THE EYES AND SAYS, “I DON'T FIND YOU SEXUALLY ATTRACTIVE ANYMORE”?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE PERSON WHO PROMISED TO LOVE YOU FOREVER LOOKS YOU IN THE EYES AND SAYS, “I DON'T FIND YOU SEXUALLY ATTRACTIVE ANYMORE”?

The confession that can shatter a marriage without ending it—and the heartbreaking truth about desire, rejection, covenant love, and the God who sees you when the person beside you no longer seems to.
There are sentences that hurt when you hear them.
And then there are sentences that move into your chest, rearrange everything you believed about yourself, and refuse to leave.
“I don't find you sexually attractive anymore.”
Seven words, depending on how they're spoken. But the damage they can do?
Sometimes years.

Imagine sitting across from the person who once couldn't wait to hold you. The person who used to reach for your hand without thinking. The person who once looked at you as though the rest of the world had disappeared.
And now they're looking at you differently.
Maybe they said it gently. Maybe they were frustrated. Maybe it came during an argument. Maybe you asked the question because you'd been feeling the distance for months.
“Do you still find me attractive?”
And for one terrible moment, they hesitated.
That hesitation told you something before their mouth ever did.
Then came the confession.
And suddenly, you weren't thinking about marriage counseling, communication, or rebuilding intimacy.
You were thinking about your stomach.
Your wrinkles.
Your weight.
Your hair.
The scars from childbirth. The changes from aging. The exhaustion that has settled into your face after years of carrying responsibilities nobody else sees.
You remembered the younger version of yourself.
The one who stood at the altar.
The one who believed that being chosen meant never having to wonder whether you were enough.
And somewhere in the silence, a question began forming that you were almost too ashamed to say aloud.
“If my own spouse doesn't want me anymore, what does that say about me?”
Stay with me, because what happens after that question can either begin the slow destruction of your marriage—or expose wounds that Jesus wants to bring into the light.
And the answer is not as simple as telling you to pray harder, lose weight, dress better, or accept that attraction disappears with age.
The Bible has something far more honest to say.
Something both confronting and healing.
Because the tragedy is not merely that your spouse's desire may have changed.
The deeper tragedy would be allowing another person's changing desire to become the final authority over your God-given worth.
And that is where we must begin.
Not with the mirror.
Not with your spouse.
But with the God who knew you before anyone ever found you beautiful.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” (KJV)
The Hebrew expression בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים (be-tselem Elohim) means “in the image of God.”
Think about what that means.
Before your wedding photographs.
Before your first kiss.
Before anyone complimented your appearance.
Before someone desired your body.
Before age, pregnancy, illness, disability, stress, or the passing years changed anything about you...
You already possessed a dignity no human being had the authority to give you.
And therefore, no human being has the authority to take it away.
You were made in God's image.
Not in the image of your spouse's preferences.
Not in the image of cultural beauty standards.
Not in the image of who you used to be twenty years ago.
Your spouse may struggle to desire you. But their struggle does not cancel your dignity.
Read that again.
Because somebody has been standing in front of a mirror, silently apologizing to themselves for growing older.
Somebody has been avoiding intimacy because rejection feels unbearable.
Somebody has been pretending not to care because admitting how much it hurts would make the pain feel even more real.
And somebody has been crying beside a sleeping spouse, wondering how two people can share the same bed and still feel so terribly alone.
Jesus sees that person.
He sees you.
But Scripture does not stop at comforting the wounded spouse.
It also confronts the person whose attraction has changed.
Because marriage was never meant to be a lifelong arrangement dependent upon the permanent preservation of youthful appearance.
When you stood before God and made your vows, you were not promising that your spouse would remain physically unchanged.
You were promising faithfulness to a real human being who would inevitably change.
Aging was always coming.
Sickness was always possible.
Exhaustion, disappointment, and seasons of emotional distance were never outside the possibilities of married life.
And if your understanding of marriage was built entirely upon physical excitement, you may have entered a covenant with the expectations of a temporary romance.
That is a dangerous foundation.
Malachi 2:14 describes marriage in striking language:
“Yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word בְּרִית (berit) means “covenant.”
A covenant is not simply a passing emotional preference.
It is a binding commitment involving faithfulness and responsibility.

In Malachi's context, God confronts men who have acted treacherously toward their wives. The passage is not teaching that spouses must manufacture sexual desire on command. It is confronting marital unfaithfulness.
And that distinction matters.
Because love and attraction are related, but they are not identical.
A person may genuinely love their spouse while experiencing a painful decline in sexual desire.
Hormonal changes can affect desire.
Depression can affect desire.
Certain medications can affect desire.
Chronic pain, unresolved conflict, emotional disconnection, trauma, exhaustion, and ongoing resentment can affect desire.
Sometimes the issue is physical.
Sometimes it is relational.
Sometimes it is psychological.
Sometimes it is a combination of several things.
And sometimes the person experiencing the change does not fully understand it themselves.
That is why the confession “I don't find you attractive anymore” should not automatically become a verdict on the marriage.
It should become the beginning of a deeper, truthful conversation.
Not an excuse for cruelty.
Not permission for infidelity.
Not an invitation to humiliate the other person.
A conversation.
Because there is an enormous difference between saying:
“You are no longer desirable.”
And saying:
“Something has changed in how I experience desire, and I don't understand it yet. I love you, and I want us to face this together.”
One statement can crush a person's sense of worth.
The other acknowledges a serious problem while protecting the dignity of the person who shares your life.
Words matter.
Especially when spoken by the person whose words carry the most weight in your heart.
Proverbs 18:21 says:
“Death and life are in the power of the tongue...” (KJV)
This is wisdom literature emphasizing the profound consequences of speech, not a claim that words possess magical power.
But anyone who has been wounded by a spouse's careless confession understands its truth.
Some sentences can remain in a marriage long after the argument ends.
And if you are the spouse who said those devastating words, please hear this.
Honesty is important.
But honesty without tenderness can become cruelty.
You are not required to pretend you feel something you do not feel.
You are responsible for how you treat the person entrusted to your care.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak “the truth in love.”
Not truth instead of love.
Not love that avoids truth.
Truth in love.
Because your spouse is not a product whose value expires when your preferences change.
Your spouse is a person.
A fellow image-bearer.
Someone with fears, vulnerabilities, memories, and a heart that may still be reaching for you even after your desire has weakened.
And before you make their body the explanation for everything that has changed, ask yourself something uncomfortable.
Have you stopped finding your spouse attractive—or have you stopped truly seeing your spouse?
There is a difference.
When was the last time you looked at them without criticizing something?
When was the last time you listened without waiting for your turn to speak?
When was the last time you noticed their sacrifices?
The hands that worked to provide.
The body that carried your children, if that is part of your story.
The shoulders that carried grief.
The eyes that stayed awake when the family was struggling.
The face that has aged beside yours.
Have you become so accustomed to their presence that you no longer recognize the extraordinary gift of being known by someone who has seen your worst days and still remains willing to walk with you?
That question may be painful.
But sometimes repentance begins with realizing that we have been treating a gift as though it were an inconvenience.
Still, we must be careful.
Not every loss of attraction is evidence of selfishness.
Not every sexually distant spouse is unloving.
And not every struggling marriage can be healed by simply deciding to appreciate one another more.
Real problems deserve real attention.
A spouse experiencing persistent loss of desire may need medical assessment, emotional support, counseling, or help addressing unresolved relational wounds.
A couple may need to rebuild trust before sexual closeness feels safe.
And if there has been coercion, betrayal, humiliation, or abuse, the solution is not to demand more physical intimacy from the wounded person.
Safety, accountability, and appropriate support matter.
Biblical faithfulness never requires someone to surrender their bodily autonomy or remain exposed to abuse.
The God who commands love does not authorize cruelty in its name.
Now consider something that many Christian couples rarely discuss honestly.
The Bible does not portray sexual desire within marriage as something dirty or unspiritual.
It recognizes its goodness.
Song of Solomon contains vivid expressions of affection, admiration, longing, and mutual delight.
In Song of Solomon 4:7, the beloved declares:
“Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.” (KJV)
This is poetic language of delighted admiration, not a theological assertion that a spouse is literally flawless.
The lover is expressing the beauty he sees in the beloved.
And perhaps that is something many marriages have forgotten.
Physical intimacy was never meant to be reduced to mechanical obligation.
It involves being welcomed.
Being cherished.
Being emotionally safe.
Being desired rather than merely tolerated.
For the spouse who has been rejected, that distinction can be heartbreaking.
Because sometimes what you miss most is not sex itself.
It's being wanted.
It's the spontaneous embrace.
The affectionate glance.
The hand resting gently on your shoulder.
The feeling that the person who knows you most intimately still delights in being near you.
And when those things disappear, the wound can reach far deeper than physical frustration.
You begin wondering whether affection has become something you must earn.
Whether you need to become thinner, younger, stronger, prettier, more successful, or more sexually adventurous just to deserve attention.
But please listen carefully.
You may work on your health. You may grow in confidence. You may address habits that affect your relationship. But you must never confuse personal growth with purchasing the right to be loved.
You are not a renovation project whose completion determines whether you deserve tenderness.
You are a human being.
And in Christ, you are called to live from grace—not from the terror of never being enough.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
The Greek expression ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν (eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn) conveys “while we were still sinners.”
Paul's point is not about sexual attractiveness or marriage.
It is about the astonishing initiative of God's love in Christ toward people who had not earned His favor.
And that truth speaks powerfully to the person who has begun measuring their entire worth by whether another human being wants them.
God's saving love was never purchased by your appearance.
Christ did not go to the cross because humanity was impressive enough to deserve Him.
He came in mercy.
He died for sinners.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered by grace.
That does not mean human rejection stops hurting.
It means human rejection is not the final word about who you are.
And if you are reading this while carrying a wound your spouse does not even realize is still bleeding, I want you to understand something.
You do not have to pretend the confession didn't hurt.
You do not have to call emotional devastation a lack of faith.
You do not have to smile through rejection to prove that you are spiritually mature.
You can grieve.
You can speak honestly.
You can say, “When you told me that, something inside me broke, and I need you to understand why.”
You can ask for patience.
You can ask for counseling.
You can ask whether your spouse is willing to work with you toward rebuilding closeness.
And you can acknowledge that healing may take time.
But there is another side of this story that must not be ignored.
What if you are the one who no longer feels attracted?
What if you still care deeply for your husband or wife, but the physical longing you once experienced has faded?
What if you are ashamed to admit it?
What if you are afraid that telling the truth will destroy the person you love?
You need more than condemnation.
You need wisdom.
Because feelings cannot always be commanded into existence.
But our responses to those feelings are moral choices.
You can choose honesty instead of deception.
Kindness instead of contempt.
Faithfulness instead of betrayal.
Curiosity instead of blame.
You can investigate what has changed without treating your spouse as defective.
You can refuse to compare them with carefully edited images, fantasies, or unrealistic expectations.
You can examine whether pornography, secret relationships, or habitual comparison have influenced your desires, without assuming those are the cause in every marriage.
You can ask whether unresolved anger has gradually poisoned affection.
You can seek qualified help.
And you can pray not merely, “Lord, make my spouse attractive to me again,” but also:
“Lord, search my heart. Show me where I have become selfish, resentful, dishonest, or unkind. Help me see my spouse truthfully and love them faithfully.”
That is a different prayer.
And it may lead to a different kind of transformation.
Psalm 139:23–24 says:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” (KJV)
Notice the posture.
Not, “God, expose everything wrong with my spouse.”
But, “Search me.”
There is something profoundly humbling about inviting God to examine the heart we have spent years defending.

And sometimes, the most important change in a marriage begins when someone stops asking, “Why aren't you enough for me?” and starts asking, “What has happened inside us—and what responsibility must I take?”
That does not guarantee restored attraction.
It does open the door to truth.
And truth is where genuine restoration must begin.
Consider 1 Corinthians 7:3–5.
Paul speaks about mutual marital responsibilities and warns spouses against unilateral, prolonged sexual deprivation, while recognizing mutual agreement and seasons of abstinence.
The Greek phrase ἐκ συμφώνου (ek symphōnou) in verse 5 means “by agreement” or “by mutual consent.”
That is significant.
Paul addresses husbands and wives with reciprocal responsibilities. The passage must not be twisted into permission for forced sex, intimidation, or the dismissal of a spouse's pain.
Sexual intimacy should never be weaponized.
Not as punishment.
Not as leverage.
Not as proof that someone is spiritually obedient.
A marriage may have genuine obligations of mutual care, but physical intimacy cannot be made loving through coercion.
And if the relationship has become a place of fear, the immediate priority is not increasing sexual frequency.
It is addressing the fear.
This is where some marriages need a very different kind of courage.
The courage to stop pretending.
The courage to admit that resentment has accumulated.
That trust has eroded.
That exhaustion has replaced tenderness.
That a husband or wife has been silently lonely for years.
And perhaps the courage to say:
“I don't know how to fix this. But I don't want us to keep hurting each other while pretending nothing is wrong.”
That sentence may not sound romantic.
But it can be the beginning of something deeply meaningful.
Because marriage restoration is not always cinematic.
Sometimes it looks like two tired people sitting in a counselor's office.
Sometimes it looks like a difficult medical appointment.
Sometimes it looks like learning to communicate without attacking.
Sometimes it looks like a spouse finally apologizing without adding excuses.
Sometimes it looks like rebuilding affectionate touch without making every embrace a demand for sex.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving a careless statement while still allowing time for trust to recover.
And sometimes it looks like acknowledging that the relationship has serious problems requiring boundaries, accountability, and outside help.
There is no biblical promise that every struggling marriage will recover its former sexual attraction.
We must not promise what Scripture does not promise.
But there is a biblical call to faithfulness, truthfulness, repentance, patience, and love.
And those things matter whether restoration happens quickly, slowly, or not in the way we hoped.
Ephesians 5:25 commands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
The Greek verb ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is a command to love.
Paul grounds the husband's responsibility in Christ's sacrificial love.
He does not say, “Love your wife as long as she looks the way she did when you married her.”
He points to Jesus.
And Jesus did not demonstrate love by exploiting weakness.
He gave Himself.
The passage also calls marriage toward reverence, holiness, and profound unity, not domination or self-serving demands.
Christ's love is not a justification for mistreatment.
It is the standard that exposes it.
And for the spouse who has been wounded, there is another essential truth.
Christlike love does not mean you must silently absorb repeated humiliation.
Forgiveness is not pretending something never happened.
Reconciliation requires truth and, where wrongdoing has occurred, meaningful repentance.
Trust is rebuilt through consistent actions.
You can forgive someone while still acknowledging that their words caused serious harm.
You can desire restoration while insisting that cruelty stop.
You can remain committed to biblical marriage while seeking protection and wise counsel when necessary.
Grace does not require denial.
And repentance is more than saying, “I'm sorry you felt that way.”
It sounds more like:
“I wounded you. I spoke carelessly. I made you feel unwanted and ashamed. I understand why that hurt, and I want to take responsibility for what I said.”
For some readers, hearing those words from a spouse would feel like rain falling on ground that has been dry for years.
But maybe your spouse has not said them.
Maybe they don't even know how.
Maybe you're still waiting.
And that brings us to one of the hardest truths in this entire conversation.
You cannot force another person to desire you, repent, or participate in rebuilding the marriage.
You can communicate.
You can pray.
You can pursue wise help.
You can take responsibility for your own behavior.
You can offer reconciliation where it is safe and appropriate.
But you cannot carry a marriage alone.
And you were never meant to make another person's response the measure of your relationship with God.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes from loving someone who no longer reaches for you.
It can make you question everything.
Your attractiveness.
Your identity.
Your future.
Even your faith.
But remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus met a Samaritan woman whose relational history was complicated. He knew the truth about her life, including her history of multiple husbands and her current relationship.
Yet He did not treat her as invisible.
He spoke to her.
He revealed Himself to her.
He offered living water.
We must not impose a story of sexual rejection onto this woman that the text never tells.
But we can recognize something unmistakable in the passage.
Jesus encountered a person with a complicated relational life and did not reduce her to that history.
He led the conversation toward truth and worship.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
You are more than the most painful thing that has happened in your marriage.
More than your spouse's opinion.
More than your body.
More than your sexual history.
More than your fear of being replaced.
You are a person whom God calls to Himself through Jesus Christ.
And even when your marriage feels uncertain, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come into the light.
Bring the grief.
Bring the anger.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the insecurity.
Bring the bitterness you have been too ashamed to confess.
Bring the secret comparisons.
Bring the unspoken resentment.
Bring the fear that you will never be desired again.
Do not pretend those things are not there.
Bring them to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not a demand that wounded people act as though they are fine.
It is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven, the brokenhearted can find comfort in God, and people can be transformed through the grace of Jesus Christ.
Not every consequence disappears.
Not every relationship is restored.
But no person who turns to Christ in faith and repentance is beyond the reach of His mercy.
And now, I want to speak to the person who has quietly been blaming themselves for everything.
Maybe your spouse's confession sent you into a desperate attempt to become desirable again.
You changed your clothes.
You changed your diet.
You changed your hairstyle.
You tried to become more affectionate.
You tried to become less demanding.
You studied every expression on their face.
You started measuring yourself against strangers.
And every time they failed to respond the way you hoped, another piece of your confidence disappeared.
Please hear this.
There is nothing wrong with caring for your body.
There is nothing wrong with pursuing physical health.
There is nothing wrong with wanting to nurture romance and attraction within marriage.
But you are not required to destroy yourself in the attempt to control another person's desires.
Your body is not your enemy.
Your age is not a moral failure.
Your scars are not evidence that you have become unworthy of tenderness.
And your spouse's loss of attraction, painful as it may be, does not prove that you have failed as a husband or wife.
You may have areas where you need to grow.
So may your spouse.
But growth should be pursued in truth, not in terror.
And if you are the spouse who has withdrawn affection, consider what your partner may be experiencing.
They may be lying awake beside you, wondering whether you regret marrying them.
They may have stopped initiating affection because they cannot bear another rejection.
They may smile in public and cry in private.
They may have begun believing that their body has become a burden to you.
You may not have intended all of that.
But if your words or behavior have contributed to that pain, love calls you to take it seriously.
Not with false promises.
Not with forced intimacy.
But with compassion, accountability, and a willingness to seek understanding together.
Because one of the cruelest things that can happen in a marriage is for one spouse to experience a wound while the other insists there is nothing to discuss.
And one of the most hopeful things that can happen is for both people to admit that something is broken without immediately deciding that the other person is the enemy.
Your spouse is not your enemy simply because desire has changed.
And you are not worthless simply because your spouse is struggling.
There may still be a path forward.
But it will require more than pretending.
It will require truth spoken with kindness.
It may require professional help.
It will require each person to take responsibility for what belongs to them.
And for Christians, it should include bringing the marriage before God with humility rather than using Scripture to win arguments.
Because Jesus Christ is not a weapon to use against your spouse.
He is Lord.
And His Word calls both of you to truth.
Perhaps tonight, the most meaningful thing you can do is sit beside your spouse and say:
“I need to talk about what happened between us. Not to attack you. Not to pressure you. But because I miss feeling close to you, and I don't want us to keep living like strangers.”
And perhaps the other person will finally answer:
“I miss us too.”
Or perhaps the conversation will reveal deeper problems.
Either way, you will have begun replacing silence with truth.
And that matters.
If you are not safe having that conversation alone, seek support from a qualified professional or a trusted person who can help you protect your well-being.
No article can diagnose your marriage from a distance.
But Scripture gives us a direction.
Love truthfully.
Repent where necessary.
Refuse cruelty.
Honor one another's dignity.
Seek wisdom.
And keep Christ at the center.
Because here is what makes the Gospel so different from the world's obsession with desirability.
The world often asks, “Are you still attractive enough to be chosen?”
The Gospel asks us to behold the Savior who came to redeem sinners who could never earn His grace.
The world says, “Stay impressive, or risk being discarded.”
Christ calls us away from building our identity upon the unstable approval of human beings.
The world can turn love into a competition of appearances.
Jesus calls His people toward sacrificial love, holiness, faithfulness, and truth.
And the cross exposes the poverty of every version of love that exists only to serve itself.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our romantic relationships.
He came to save sinners.
Through His death and resurrection, He accomplished what no human relationship could ever accomplish: reconciliation with God for those who trust in Him.
That is the foundation.
Marriage is precious.
But marriage is not your savior.
Sexual attraction is a meaningful gift.
But attraction is not your god.
Your spouse's affection matters.
But it cannot carry the full weight of your identity.
Only Christ belongs at the center of that place.
And when He is there, you can face painful truths without surrendering your entire worth to them.
You can grieve without believing you are worthless.
You can repent without believing you are beyond redemption.
You can pursue restoration without pretending that restoration is guaranteed.
You can love faithfully without calling abuse love.
You can hope without lying to yourself.
And you can trust that the Lord remains worthy of worship even when your marriage is passing through a season you never imagined.
That is not shallow optimism.
That is faith learning to stand in the middle of uncertainty.
And perhaps that is the message someone in your family needs tonight.
Not another perfect photograph of a smiling couple.
Not another Christian slogan that ignores complicated pain.
But an honest reminder that marriages involve real people, real bodies, real wounds, real choices, and a real need for the grace of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to reveal intimate details about your spouse or expose private conversations.
You can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Or if you are struggling to find the courage to have an honest conversation, comment, “Pray for our marriage.”

And if God has helped you and your spouse rebuild closeness after a painful season, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading your words may need the encouragement that change is possible, even when it takes time and hard work.
Not because every marriage can be repaired with a few paragraphs, but because you may need to return to these truths on a night when rejection feels louder than faith.
You may never know which married couple is silently struggling behind a beautiful family picture.
Which husband has stopped believing he is wanted.
Which wife has been crying over the changes in her body.
Which spouse is carrying guilt over a confession they wish they had expressed differently.
A thoughtful share may help someone find the courage to seek a healthier conversation, professional support, or renewed dependence upon Christ.
Sometimes sending an article privately is the kinder act.
We are here to speak about the realities people often hide behind their Sunday smiles.
Marriage.
Shame.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Temptation.
Loneliness.
Healing.
And above all, the redeeming grace of Jesus Christ.
Because we believe discipleship should not end when the church service is over.
It should reach the kitchen table.
The hospital room.
The exhausted parent.
The struggling marriage.
The person quietly wondering whether God still sees them.
Not out of guilt.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
But because supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful way to serve others for His glory.
Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who minister the Word. Philippians 4:15–18 records Paul's gratitude for the Philippians' financial partnership in his ministry.
Paul describes their gift as an offering pleasing to God.
That gives us a beautiful picture of voluntary generosity.
These free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter Scripture, hear the Gospel, and be pointed toward Jesus Christ.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still make a difference.
Pray for this ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Speak truth with love.
And keep pointing people to Christ.
Because the mission is bigger than a platform.
Bigger than any one article.
It is about Jesus being known, His Word being heard, and wounded people discovering that grace is not merely a beautiful religious word.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners, revealed supremely through Jesus Christ.
And when that grace takes hold of a life, it changes how we confess, forgive, love, endure, and begin again.
So, to the spouse who no longer feels attractive...
To the husband who misses being desired...
To the wife who no longer recognizes herself in the mirror...
To the person whose heart sank when their spouse finally told the truth...
And to the spouse who wants to find a way back but does not know where to begin...
Do not allow this painful chapter to become the entire definition of your story.
Seek truth.
Seek wisdom.
Seek help when you need it.
Repent where you have sinned.
Extend grace without abandoning necessary boundaries.
And bring your broken places to Jesus.
Because He is not frightened by the conversations you are afraid to have.
He is not surprised by the weakness you have been hiding.
And He does not ask you to pretend that your wounds are healed when they are not.
He calls you to Himself.
Maybe your marriage will find renewed tenderness.
Maybe rebuilding trust will take longer than you hoped.
Maybe you will need to confront realities you have spent years avoiding.
But whatever happens next, do not forget the truth that existed before your spouse ever chose you.
You were created in God's image.
And the invitation to find forgiveness, new life, and lasting hope in Jesus Christ remains open.
The person you love may no longer look at you the way they once did—but the cross still declares that your deepest worth was never theirs to decide.
